newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Price rise fears fuel SAfrica spending, investment.
newsitem.headline: Price rise fears fuel SAfrica spending, investment.

text.p: Pre-emptive buying ahead of price rises expected to follow the sharp fall in the rand since February fuelled both private sector expenditure, investment and inventories in the second quarter, the Reserve Bank said.

Growth in aggregate real gross domestic expenditure -- traditionally a volatile figure -- jumped to a seasonally adjusted and annualised rate of nine percent in the three months to June after a fall of 1.5 percent in the first quarter.
This turnabout was due to an acceleration in real private consumption expenditure and a sudden sharp increase in inventory accumulation, the Bank said in its Quarterly Bulletin.
Private consumption expenditure rose four percent in the second quarter from three percent in the first, with household spending on consumer goods and services jumping 13.5 percent.

"Higher purchases of transport equipment, motivated strongly by expectations of future price increases that may arise from the depreciation of the exchange rate of the rand, were primarily responsible for the sharp increase in real consumer spending on durable goods," it said.
Real gross domestic fixed investment slowed down from an annualised seven percent in the first quarter, but remained relatively high at 5.5 percent in the second quarter.

Private sector fixed investment, which had declined progressively from 8.5 in the third quarter of 1995 to three percent in the first quarter of 1996, reverted back to 6.5 percent growth in the second quarter.
All major sectors saw an increase, except mining, with agriculture prominent. Once again, capital spending appeared to have been spurred by a desire to pre-empt price rises, the Bank said.
"Of particular significance is that a sizeable portion of the new production capacity in private manufacturing was meant for the enhancement of South Africa's export potential," it added.
The slowdown in real investment in inventories since the second quarter of 1995 was reversed in the second quarter of 1996.

"Whereas the change in real inventory investment lowered the growth rate of real gross domestic product by five percentage points in the first quarter of 1996, it added 4.5 percentage points to overall growth in the second quarter," the Bank noted.
The increase in stocks reflected a jump in crude oil and other merchandise goods, again ahead of expected price rises.
